Duodecimo, with frontispiece portrait of Leichhardt, complete with half-title and advertisement leaves in worn original printed papered boards. Melbourne, Published by J.T. Hendy, Printed by W. Bunce wrote one of two ‘essential’ primary accounts of Leichhardt’s second expedition, 1846-7, published later by participants (the other is by John F. Mann). Leichhardt himself published no account of his failed second expedition to cross the continent. Bunce appended to his own journal a heavily edited – virtually rewritten – version of Leichhardt’s narrative of his third expedition, August – September 1847. description: SOUTH AUSTRALIAN ASSOCIATION. SOUTH AUSTRALIA. OUTLINE OF THE PLAN OF A PROPOSED COLONY to be founded on the South Coast of Australia; with an Account of the soil, climate, rivers, &c. With Maps. Octavo, with three folding handcoloured engraved maps; a fine uncut copy in later marbled wrappers, Davidson copy with bookplate. London, Ridgway and Sons, 1834. Rare: the foundation of South Australia. The South Australian Land Company was formed in 1831 but was soon after disbanded when the company was unable to secure a Royal Charter. The same individuals, who continued to be inspired mainly by the theoretical proposals of Edward Gibbon Wakefield and the economic theory of self-supporting colonisation proposed by Robert Torrens, reformed in 1834 as the South Australian Association, having the same objects as the earlier company: “to found a Colony, under Royal Charter, and without convict labour, … on the South Coast of Australia, a tract of country far removed from the existing penal settlements”. The present proposal, or perhaps prospectus, seeks support for establishing the Association, providing a detailed description of the area between 132° and 141° East on the south coast with an account of its productive capacity, as well as concrete proposals for the formation of a colony along the theoretical lines recommended by Wakefield in 1829. The final 60 pages of this 80-page pamphlet are notable in their own right. In this portion of the pamphlet the editor prints extracts from many authoritative sources to support the case for settlement. Most important among these is a detailed seven-page report by Captain Sutherland of his seven-month sealing expedition in 1819 in the Governor Macquarie based on Kangaroo Island. One of the earliest extended accounts of sealing activity on the south coast, Sutherland’s 1819 report is here greatly extended by the transcript of a more recent interview with him. Printed in question and answer form, this interview is over six pages in length. Further interviews are printed here, again in question and answer form. Among those interviewed are William Westall, Chevalier Peter Dillon, George Goold (Master of HMS Dryad), and a handful of others. Further, there are long extracts from the published works of other authorities including Matthew Flinders (sixteen pages), François Péron (nine pages), and Charles Sturt (seven pages). description: WALLIS, James. AN HISTORICAL ACCOUNT OF THE COLONY OF NEW SOUTH WALES and its Dependent Settlements; in illustration of Twelve Views, engraved by W. Rare: the first book of general landscape views of early New South Wales, representing the first great celebration of the progress in the colony made under the civilising rule of Governor Macquarie. It is also the first plate book, properly so called, to consist entirely of plates engraved in the colony by a colonial engraver. Engraved in Newcastle, New South Wales, where Wallis was Commandant, by the convict artist William Preston who had earlier worked for Absalom West, the plates show scenes in Sydney, Newcastle and the Hawkesbury River, as well as an Aboriginal corroboree, and plates of kangaroos and black swans. “Wallis’s book has a most important position in a collection of Australian plate books. It is the first book of general landscape views of early New South Wales, representing the first great celebration of the progress in the colony made under the civilising rule of Governor Macquarie and, indeed, of Wallis himself. It is also the first plate book, properly so called, to consist entirely of plates engraved in the colony by a colonial engraver ... Wallis’s book of views should be in every serious collection of Australian plate books” (Wantrup). The present copy includes the additional leaf reprinting Macquarie’s highly commendatory “General Order”, published in the Sydney Gazette when the 46th Regiment was recalled in 1818, praising Wallis’s work in improving Newcastle and his humane treatment of the convicts there. title: BONWICK, James. NOTES OF A GOLD DIGGER AND GOLD DIGGERS’ GUIDE. Duodecimo, with handcoloured map of “Routes to the Victo
description: BONWICK, James. NOTES OF A GOLD DIGGER AND GOLD DIGGERS’ GUIDE. Duodecimo, with handcoloured map of “Routes to the Victoria Diggings” and engraved plate “Diggers” (both with an old central fold), three small patches replaced on plate, expert repairs to margins of several leaves, a clean copy without wrappers in modern calf, gilt. Melbourne, R. Connebee, 1852. Rare and much prized. This appealing diggers’ guidebook, the first Victorian publication on the diggings, was written by Bonwick after he had failed at the diggings. He published this little work in September 1852 for the use of newly arrived hopefuls. Bonwick had a flair for elucidation, which makes this slim duodecimo a thorough, well-presented and still very readable exposition of life and work at the diggings. The 42 pages of closely-printed text commence with a descriptive itinerary of the trip from Melbourne to the diggings. The major component is entitled “The Digger at Work” and its complement, “The Digger at Home”. These are spirited and instructive accounts of conditions on the goldfields, illustrated with lively anecdote and advice drawn from the author’s experience. A dedicated social improver, Bonwick introduced further sections entitled “Health at the Diggings” and “Moral State of the Diggings”. His very full booklet concludes with a section on the history of gold discovery in Australia and another on the geology of the Victorian diggings. Bonwick’s Notes of a Gold Digger is a classic of goldfields literature. An attractive and evocative pamphlet, it is illustrated by a handcoloured map of “Routes to the Victoria Diggings” and a frontispiece, entitled “Diggers”, both engraved by Samuel Calvert. description: BONWICK, James. WESLEYAN METHODISM IN SOUTH AUSTRALIA. 18mo (irregularly signed), original printed wrappers, later plain cloth. Adelaide, Printed by T. Strode, [1851]. Very rare: one of Bonwick’s earliest works. This ephemeral piece, as with almost all Bonwick’s books published during his years in South Australia, was issued in comparatively small numbers to an audience that was singularly uninterested in the published book – a constant subject of complaint among mid-century South Australian writers. Ferguson 7189; Pescott, 9. Estimate $200/300

title: BONWICK, James. WESTERN VICTORIA; its Geography, Geology, and Social Condition.
description: BONWICK, James. WESTERN VICTORIA; its Geography, Geology, and Social Condition. The Narrative of an Educational Tour in 1857. Duodecimo in sixes, frontispiece by Samuel Calvert, other engravings in the text by Calvert, one leaf with a repaired tear, some pencilled marks in the margins, plain rebacking to original (blue) papered boards, paper strengthening of hinges: with two loosely inserted manuscript notes by E. E. Pescott, and a homemade dustwrapper. Geelong, Thomas Brown, n.d., circa 1858. Rare: the first and best early historical tour of the rich Western District of Victoria, from the Barwon to Mt. Gambier. This is one of the most sought after and interesting of Bonwick’s many books. The final chapter includes an account of the Linton Diggings and its social conditions. The pagination is irregular, with page numbers 141-4 repeated without interrupting the text; the book collates regularly by signatures, however. See Ferguson 7217 (miscollated); Pescott, 40 (miscollated). Estimate $600/800

title: BONWICK. BEDDOW, Mrs. E.A. APPRECIATIONS OF JAMES BONWICK. Born 1817. Died 1906… Octavo, with a portrait of Bonwick, ori
description: BONWICK. BEDDOW, Mrs. E.A. APPRECIATIONS OF JAMES BONWICK. Born 1817. description: ANGAS, George French (illustrated by). A VISIT TO AUSTRALIA AND ITS GOLD REGIONS. First edition: the text is drawn from various sources; the very numerous steel-engraved vignettes throughout are almost certainly after George French Angas. An important early annual compilation and the first such volume prepared for the gold colony. Extending very far beyond mere statistics, it is more of a highly detailed ‘Year Book’ of the Colony of Victoria (into which Archer’s series did, indeed, eventually transmute over ensuing decades). title: EARP, G. Butler. THE GOLD COLONIES OF AUSTRALIA: Comprising Their History, Territorial Divisions, Produce, and Capabilit
description: EARP, G. Butler. THE GOLD COLONIES OF AUSTRALIA: Comprising Their History, Territorial Divisions, Produce, and Capabilities; Also, Ample Notices of the Gold Mines, and How to Get to Them; With Advice to Emigrants... Enlarged and Corrected Edition. Octavo, folding frontispiece map, original printed yellow papered boards (rubbed) rebacked. London, Geo Routledge & Co., 1852. Third edition. One of the most popular of the gold digger’s guides, with tens of thousands of copies printed over 1852-3, it is based substantially on letters received from the goldfields, many of which are quoted extensively, and on the author’s wide personal experience of the colonies. Ferguson 9356; Wantrup 367 (first edition). Estimate $100/200

title: GILKS, Edward. THE DIGGER’S ROAD GUIDE, to the Gold Mines of Victoria, and the Country Extending 210 Miles, round Melbourne.
description: GILKS, Edward. THE DIGGER’S ROAD GUIDE, to the Gold Mines of Victoria, and the Country Extending 210 Miles, round Melbourne. Carefully Compiled from Authentic Sources & Lithographed by Edwd. Gilks. Lithographed map within borders, handcoloured in outline, printed area 195 x 255 mm, small vignette inset, mounted, framed, and glazed. Melbourne, Published by S. Leigh, August 1853. Rare and highly ephemeral: the very rare handcoloured issue of this highly detailed and accurate map of the colony, issued separately and sold for 2/6. Showing the major diggings, roads, townships, squatting routes and runs, halting places, natural features, and so on. This is the only such digger’s pocket-size road map to have been produced by a recognised gold rush artist. Edward Gilks – one of the founders of the Victorian Fine Arts Society – worked as a commercial engraver in Melbourne after arriving from England in January 1853. Not in Tooley; Wantrup 395. Estimate $4000/6000

title: MACPHERSON, Emma. MY EXPERIENCES IN AUSTRALIA. Being Recollections of a Visit to the Australian Colonies in 1856-7. By a Lady.
description: MACPHERSON, Emma. MY EXPERIENCES IN AUSTRALIA. Being Recollections of a Visit to the Australian Colonies in 1856-7. By a Lady. Octavo, with six lithographed plates (not entirely conforming to List of Illustrations), sewing loosening, original gilt-decorated violet cloth, spine faded. London, J.F. Hope, 1860. First edition and extremely scarce. An account of life in Australia when Emma Macpherson accompanied her husband, Allan (the future Laird of Blairgowrie), to his property in New South Wales. She gives a good, if pessimistic, account of rural and city life, while her account of their long overland journey through New South Wales in the late gold-rush is interesting and useful. The plates in this volume are after the author’s own drawings and her sketchbook, which includes the originals of four of the six lithographs that appear in this book is in the Mitchell Library.
